summary: This standards-track document describes a port mapping that lets RTP receivers choose ports for an auxiliary unicast session in applications that use multicast and unicast. It guards against denial-of-service and amplification attacks.

eli5.summary: Receivers pick their own mailbox for private replies, so nobody can trick a sender into mailing junk to a victim.

questions: how does the rtp token work
what is the rtcp token packet type
subtitle: How a receiver mixing multicast and unicast RTP picks its own ports without letting an attacker aim traffic at someone else.

tldr.problem: In a multicast RTP application, ports are fixed in advance, but an auxiliary unicast session (for example a retransmission) needs ports chosen by the receiver. Without protection, an attacker could trick a server into sending RTP packets to a victim.
tldr.mechanism: The server hands the client an opaque Token tied to the client's IP address, a client-chosen nonce and an expiry time. The client attaches the Token to RTCP messages that trigger or control the unicast session, and the server validates it.
tldr.outcome: The client can use any receive ports it likes, and an off-path attacker cannot redirect the unicast flow. The protection is weaker if the attacker holds a valid Token and can spoof the victim's address.

today: RFC 6284 is a Proposed Standard from June 2011. The unit metadata shows no obsoleting or updating RFC.

sections.title: Mixing Multicast and Unicast RTP
sections.content:
In multicast RTP applications the destination ports are defined declaratively: receivers cannot choose them, and senders use the predefined ports. In unicast RTP the receiver must choose its own ports, because they are local resources and NAT devices are commonly deployed, so static port assignments cannot be used.

The trouble starts when one application uses both. Examples in the RFC are a receiver sending unicast RTCP NACK feedback to a retransmission server that resends missing packets over unicast, and rapid acquisition of a new multicast session through unicast burst packets (RFC 6285). The usual way to agree on ports is the SDP Offer/Answer Model (RFC 3264), but that needs extra exchanges, which adds delay and burdens a server running many unicast sessions.

This RFC defines port mapping: receivers choose their own UDP ports for each unicast session when offer/answer is not available. It does not apply when TCP is the transport of the unicast session.
sections.eli5: Some mail goes to a fixed mailbox that everybody knows. Other mail has to go to a mailbox you pick yourself. This RFC lets you pick your own mailbox safely when you get both kinds.

sections.title: The Token-Based Design
sections.content:
The server gives the client a Token, an opaque value based on the client's IP address as seen by the server, a time-to-live and a random nonce provided by the client. Using it takes two steps: request and retrieve a Token, then establish the unicast session.

A Token can be reused for all unicast sessions with that server until it expires. By default Tokens are server specific, but several servers sharing the same secret key and algorithm, and loosely synchronized clocks, can accept the same Token. A Token becomes invalid if the client's IP address (as the server sees it) changes or the server expires it, and then the client must request a new one.

When the client wants a unicast session, it includes the Token with its RTCP feedback message. The server checks that the IP address information matches. If validation fails, the server tells the client and no unicast session is set up. This is why an attacker cannot simply spoof another client's address and start a unicast transmission to random clients.
sections.eli5: The shop gives you a ticket with your address sealed inside. When you ask for a parcel you show the ticket, and the shop only sends it if the ticket matches where the request came from.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
The RFC uses an example with a retransmission server. Ports P1 and P2 are the multicast RTP and RTCP ports. P3 is the server's RTCP port for feedback, and the port the server uses to send unicast RTP and RTCP sender reports. P4 is the server port for receiver reports in the unicast session. PT is the server port for Token requests. The client picks its own ports *c0, *c1, *c2 and *cT.

  • The client learns the server address and ports (P3, P4, PT) from the session description. P4 MUST differ from P3; PT MAY equal P3.
  • If it has no valid Token, the client sends a Port Mapping Request from port cT to port PT. The server builds a Token and answers with a Port Mapping Response from PT to cT.
  • The client attaches the Token to RTCP feedback that triggers or controls the unicast session. If the Token is invalid or missing, the server sends a Token Verification Failure.
  • The unicast session exists only after the server receives a feedback message with a valid Token that it must react to. From then on, ordinary RTP and RTCP rules from RFC 3550 apply.

It is strongly RECOMMENDED that the client uses the same port for c0 and c1. Periodic RTCP receiver reports sent from c0 then keep the NAT binding alive for the incoming unicast traffic, and it conserves NAT port bindings. Server-to-client RTP and RTCP in the unicast session MUST be multiplexed on one port (RFC 5761). The client MUST use the same RTCP CNAME in both sessions, and it MUST be unique (RFC 6222), so the server can correlate reports.

RTP flows only from server to client in the unicast session. A client that needs to send RTP back must use regular session establishment such as RFC 3264.

A client SHOULD use separate receive ports for subsequent unicast sessions, to avoid packet leakage from an earlier session. After two minutes, a previously used port can be reused.
sections.eli5: You ask for a ticket first, then show the ticket whenever you order something. You also keep using the same doorbell for the regular mail and the special deliveries so the postman does not forget your house.

sections.title: The TOKEN RTCP Messages
sections.content:
A new RTCP control packet type, TOKEN (210), carries four messages told apart by the sub-message type (SMT) field. Integers are in network byte order, and Reserved fields SHALL be set to zero and ignored.

  • Port Mapping Request (SMT=1): sent by the client to ask for a Token. It carries a 64-bit random nonce, which must stay the same in duplicate copies of one request but be new for every new request.
  • Port Mapping Response (SMT=2): sent by the server. It carries the requesting client's SSRC, the associated nonce, a Token element, a 64-bit absolute expiration time (an NTP timestamp), a 32-bit relative expiration time and a Packet Types element listing the RTCP packet types that need a Token.
  • Token Verification Request (SMT=3): accompanies an RTCP message and carries the associated nonce, the Token element and the associated absolute expiration time. The client MUST NOT send it with an expired Token.
  • Token Verification Failure (SMT=4): sent by the server when the Token was invalid or missing. It names the failed packet type and FMT value so the client can tell which of its messages was rejected.

A relative expiration time of zero means the server declined to grant a Token. The server sends the relative time in the clear so the client can ask for a new Token well before expiry. If the server later changes which packet types need a Token, it SHALL NOT send a new Port Mapping Response to existing clients, which find out when a failure message arrives. A large Token can make the RTCP packet bigger than the MTU, and some NATs and middleboxes do not pass IP fragments.
sections.eli5: There are four little notes: please give me a ticket, here is your ticket, here is my ticket with my order, and sorry, your ticket was no good.

sections.title: Building and Checking Tokens
sections.content:
The Token format is private to the server and opaque to the client. Implementations MUST encode at least the client's IP address as seen by the server, the client's 64-bit nonce and the 64-bit absolute expiration time. The RECOMMENDED construction is HMAC-SHA1 (RFC 2104) over those values joined together. The HMAC key MUST be at least 160 bits long and come from a cryptographically secure random source (RFC 4086). A stronger HMAC such as HMAC-SHA256 could replace it if HMAC-SHA1 were compromised.

The server SHOULD occasionally choose a new key, and a key-id placed in front of the hash lets it reject Tokens made with an old key without computing the HMAC. Expiry has to be chosen with care: Tokens valid for an unnecessarily long time, for example several hours, might impose security risks, while shorter lifetimes mean clients fetch Tokens more often.

To validate, the server repeats its own construction using the client's IP address and the nonce and expiration time reported in the Token Verification Request, then compares the result with the Token. It is valid if they match and the expiration time has not passed. A changed IP address, a wrong nonce or wrong expiry makes validation fail, and the server MUST then reply with a Token Verification Failure.

If a client gets an invalid Token (relative expiration of zero) or a verification failure twice for the same request, it SHOULD check whether the session description has been updated and then back off exponentially from the third attempt on. Applications should also define their own error response; for RAMS this RFC adds code 405 Invalid Token.
sections.eli5: The shop seals your address and an expiry date into the ticket with a secret stamp only the shop owns. Anyone can look at the ticket, but nobody can forge one that the stamp will accept.

sections.title: SDP Signaling
sections.content:
The media-level SDP attribute portmapping-req tells clients where to get a Token. Its form is a=portmapping-req: followed by a port and, optionally, a network type, address type and connection address. Only unicast addresses SHOULD be used for the optional address. If no address is given, the address in the applicable c line is used.

Its presence means a Token MUST be included in certain RTCP messages that trigger or control the unicast session, and that the client MUST receive the unicast RTP and RTCP on the port it used to send the triggering message. In an offer/answer exchange, an answerer that supports the scheme MUST echo the attribute back with the same port and address. One that does not simply ignores it and can join the multicast session but cannot use the Token-protected unicast service.

The use of SDP requires support for the SDP grouping framework with FID semantics (RFC 5888), the RTP/AVPF profile (RFC 4585) and the rtcp-mux attribute.
sections.eli5: A note in the program guide says which counter to visit for your ticket, so every viewer knows where to go.

sections.title: Limits of the Protection
sections.content:
A Token protects against off-path denial-of-service attacks: an attacker using one IP address cannot make RTP packets flow to a victim with a different address. It is vulnerable to replay if the attacker obtains a valid Token for the victim and can spoof the victim's source address. That is especially easy when attacker and victim share an address behind a large-scale NAT.

Multicast runs on managed networks, which choose whether to use ingress filtering (RFC 2827). Where it is off, a server can shorten the window by expiring Tokens quickly, even so quickly that the client must fetch one right before use, at the cost of delay.

On-path attackers can alter fields in the Port Mapping Response or Token Verification Request. Changing fields used in Token construction just makes validation fail. Changing the relative expiration time still validates, so it can only be spotted by monitoring the server. If this is a concern, RTCP SHOULD be protected with SRTCP (RFC 3711). A server MUST NOT use the Token secret key for other purposes. The SDP description itself needs integrity protection and source authentication, since an interceptor could redirect Token requests by changing the port.

Address-pooling NATs can hand a host a different public IPv4 address after all its mappings expire, which invalidates the Token and costs one extra round trip. Regular RTCP receiver reports sent for the multicast session prevent this.
sections.eli5: The ticket stops strangers far away from tricking the shop. It does not stop someone who steals your ticket and pretends to live at your house, so tickets should expire quickly.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registers the portmapping-req SDP attribute at media level, and the RTCP packet type TOKEN with value 210. A new registry, SMT Values for TOKEN Packet Type, is managed under IETF Review. The SMT field is five bits, allowing 32 values. Values 0 and 31 are reserved, 1 to 4 are the four messages, and 5 to 30 are unassigned. The RFC also adds code 405, Invalid Token, to the RAMS Response Code Space Registry, used when the Token in a RAMS-R message is invalid.
sections.eli5: The official list of numbers gets a new entry for these tickets, and some spare slots are left for future ideas.
